passage: Payal, come and sit. Vandana Aunty will tell you about her first Diwali. I was twenty-four. In front of ten guests my mother-in-law said my rotis were like leather. Everyone looked at me. My own sister whispered, "Say something back!" My face burned. But I said, "I'll learn from you, Ji," and passed the sabzi. I did not join the laughing, and I did not say a word against her. That night I told my husband Arun, "That hurt me in front of everyone. Help me think what to do." He spoke to his mother the next day, quietly. Things were not perfect after, but the guests never saw two women fighting, and Arun and I stayed on the same side. You don't have to swallow everything, beta. Choose where you say it.

qa.q: How many guests were at the Diwali meal?
What was Vandana feeling when everyone looked at her, and what cue does she give?
qa.a: She felt hurt and embarrassed, since she says her face burned.

qa.q: What did Vandana do that night, and why might it help?
qa.a: She told her husband Arun privately that it hurt and asked for his help. A private talk keeps the couple on the same side without a public fight.

qa.q: Why might Vandana's sister have whispered "Say something back!"?
qa.a: Her sister probably wanted to defend her and saw silence as weakness, while Vandana chose not to answer sharply in front of guests.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how she avoided taking sides publicly against her in-laws and raised the hurt privately with her husband.
